One customer's script created 40,000 orders in ten minutes last week and slowed every other customer down. I want to add rate limiting to `src/server.ts` and ship it this week.

What we have:

- 3 instances of `src/server.ts` behind a round-robin load balancer.
- A Redis 7 cluster already used for sessions by another service; we may use it.
- `POST /orders` writes to Postgres and is the expensive call; `GET /orders` is cheap.
- About 20 enterprise customers have scripted integrations that legitimately burst.

Not decided yet:

- What to key the limit on: `x-customer-id`, client IP, or both.
- Algorithm: fixed window, sliding window, or token bucket.
- Where counters live: Redis, or in each instance's memory.
- What happens if the counter store is unreachable: let requests through or reject them.
- How enterprise customers get higher limits, and who owns those numbers.
- What a rejected client sees.
- How to roll it out without breaking the enterprise integrations.

content.text: Round 1 of the design tree. Facts I pulled from the repo: `x-customer-id` is an unverified client header, there is no Redis client or package manifest, and `GET /orders` returns an unbounded result set.

content.name: ask

questions.question: Is the plan's target right — should this week's change be a limiter sized against DB capacity, plus a bounded GET /orders?

brief.where: PLAN.md says one customer made 40,000 orders in ten minutes and slowed everyone. src/server.ts writes every POST straight to Postgres in the request path; src/orders.ts returns every order for a customer with no limit or pagination. 40,000/600s ≈ 67 inserts/s — modest for Postgres, while a GET from that customer now returns up to 40k rows per call. No package.json, tests, or pool configuration exist in the repo.
brief.what: Whether a rate limiter on /orders addresses the mechanism that actually starved other customers, and what number the limit is sized against. The code cannot settle this: it depends on how the slowdown showed up in production (write latency, pool exhaustion, or slow reads for the now-huge customer).
brief.how: The answer fixes whether round 2 sizes a per-customer budget in requests/second, whether GET is capped too, and whether a write-concurrency cap is in scope this week rather than a counter store.

evidence.note: the stated symptom and the open list
POST writes inline; GET returns whatever the DB gives
unbounded select for one customer

risks: A limiter tuned to a guessed number either never fires or fires on the 20 legitimate bursters.
If the real mechanism is read amplification or pool exhaustion, shipping the limiter leaves the outage reproducible.

options.label: Limiter plus bounded GET /orders
options.description: Rate-limit writes and cap/paginate the read path in the same change
options.tradeoff: Fixes the amplification that most plausibly starved neighbours, and gives the limiter a number to defend; costs a pagination change that enterprise integrations may also rely on.
options.holds_when: You have production evidence that the blowup coincided with one customer's data volume or write rate.
options.cost: Two files touched, one API contract change, plus a migration/index if reads are the cause.

options.label: Rate limiter only, as written
options.description: Ship exactly the plan: counters on POST /orders
options.tradeoff: Smallest diff and fastest to ship; leaves unbounded reads and any connection-pool exhaustion untouched, so the same customer can still degrade everyone at a lower request rate.
options.holds_when: You know the slowdown tracked insert rate, not data volume.

options.label: DB write-concurrency cap first
options.description: Queue or shed writes above a fixed in-flight count, per instance
options.tradeoff: Protects Postgres regardless of who is calling and needs no identity key; gives no per-customer fairness and is more invasive surgery than a limiter.
options.holds_when: The symptom was pool exhaustion or write latency, and fairness between customers is a later goal.

questions.question: Can x-customer-id be trusted as a rate-limit key — i.e. does the edge strip and set it?

brief.where: src/server.ts reads x-customer-id from the incoming request and rejects only when it is absent. Nothing in the repo verifies it, and any budget keyed on it is chosen by the caller. The three instances sit behind a round-robin balancer, so the client IP is visible only if the balancer preserves it.
brief.what: Whether the header is authenticated upstream, which decides if it can carry a per-customer budget at all. This is an infrastructure fact only you can confirm — the repo contains no gateway config.
brief.how: If the edge guarantees the header, key on customer id and the 20 enterprise overrides attach to a real identity. If not, v1 keys on client IP and records customer id for reporting; authentication becomes its own ticket.

evidence.note: presence check, no authentication

risks: An untrusted key means one loop with a random header defeats the limiter entirely.
IP keying breaks per-customer fairness for enterprises behind a shared egress.

options.label: Key on x-customer-id, edge-verified
options.description: Edge/gateway overwrites the header from the authenticated session
options.tradeoff: Correct fairness key, matches the existing 401 contract, and makes per-customer tiers meaningful; only valid if you can point at the config that overwrites the header.
options.holds_when: The balancer or an upstream gateway strips client-supplied values for this header.
options.cost: None beyond confirming the edge behaviour.

options.label: Key on client IP until a header is authenticated
options.description: Shard on source address for v1
options.tradeoff: Cannot be forged at layer 7 and ships this week; punishes customers sharing NAT and gives the 20 bursters no individual budget.
options.holds_when: The header is unauthenticated and you need enforcement now.

options.label: Both: IP cap plus customer-id cap
options.description: Two budgets, each with its own number
options.tradeoff: Catches spoofed ids and shared-NAT abuse; doubles the numbers you must choose and explain, and makes a 429 ambiguous for support.
options.holds_when: You expect deliberate evasion, not just one runaway script.

options.label: Authenticate the header in this release
options.description: Make customer id real before limiting on it
options.tradeoff: Turns the header into a trustworthy key; almost certainly blows the one-week scope and forces every integration to change its client.
options.holds_when: There is already a token/credential scheme the integrations can adopt quickly.

questions.question: Should counters live in the shared Redis cluster under a namespaced key prefix, with in-memory only as a fallback?

brief.where: Three instances behind round-robin. There is no Redis client anywhere in the repo; src/db.ts is the only external dependency. The Redis 7 cluster exists but belongs to the sessions service, so using it is a cross-team grant, not a local decision.
brief.what: Where the counters live. Per-instance memory turns a published 100 rps limit into roughly 33 rps per instance with round-robin jitter, and a restart forgets the window.
brief.how: Redis needs a keyspace grant, a client dependency, and an atomic check-and-increment (Lua or INCR-with-TTL) on the hot path. Memory needs no infra but cannot enforce a cluster-wide number.

evidence.note: three instances, shared Redis, expensive POST
the only external client today

risks: Borrowed keyspace: another team's failover or eviction policy becomes your limiter's availability.
Lua scripting on a cluster requires all keys in one slot — a per-customer key prefix must keep hash tags consistent.

options.label: Redis, namespaced prefix, atomic Lua
options.description: Shared cluster, keys like rl:{orders}:<customer>
options.tradeoff: One cluster-wide number that survives restarts and LB roulette; costs a cross-team keyspace grant, a new dependency, and hash-tag discipline on a cluster.
options.holds_when: The sessions owners will give you a dedicated database index and a no-eviction guarantee.
options.cost: Client dependency, permission ticket, one Lua script.

options.label: Per-instance memory
options.description: Local counters in each process
options.tradeoff: No infra work and no cross-team dependency; the effective limit is three times the number you publish and varies with load-balancer luck, and every deploy resets it.
options.holds_when: A rough ceiling is enough and you accept 3x overshoot.

options.label: Memory counters synced to Redis periodically
options.description: Fast local path, batch reconciliation
options.tradeoff: Keeps the hot path dependency-free while approaching a global number; state is approximate and drift bugs are hard to reproduce.
options.holds_when: Redis round-trips are shown to be a latency problem, which they probably are not at 67 rps.

questions.question: On a counter-store outage, should requests pass with a per-instance local bucket as the degraded ceiling (not unlimited)?

brief.where: Redis would become a new hard dependency in the POST path. Today a Postgres outage fails the request, but a counter outage would newly fail requests Postgres could have served.
brief.what: What the limiter does when Redis is unreachable. This decides the blast radius of someone else's Redis incident on your revenue writes.
brief.how: Unlimited fail-open removes protection exactly when a failover spike is plausible; a local fallback keeps a ceiling; fail-closed turns a Redis incident into an orders outage.

evidence.note: the write path the limiter would wrap

risks: Fail-open unlimited is a free pass during the exact window the abusive client is most damaging.
Fail-closed makes another team's Redis availability a prerequisite for taking orders.

options.label: Fail-open with a local fallback bucket
options.description: Redis down: each instance enforces a rough local cap
options.tradeoff: Never rejects a paying customer for infra we own, while keeping a ceiling during an incident; the degraded cap is 3x sloppy and must be documented as approximate.
options.holds_when: You want availability first but not a complete free pass.
options.cost: A second code path and a metric to prove it engaged.

options.label: Fail-open, no limit
options.description: Counter errors are logged and ignored
options.tradeoff: Simplest and never punishes customers; the runaway script gets unrestricted access during any Redis blip.
options.holds_when: Protection is a fairness nicety rather than a capacity guard.

options.label: Fail-closed 503
options.description: Reject when the counter cannot be read
options.tradeoff: Guarantees the cap and is easy to reason about; converts another team's Redis failover into your downtime.
options.holds_when: Overload is genuinely worse than rejection, e.g. the DB will fall over.

questions.question: Should a throttled call return 429 with Retry-After plus X-RateLimit-* headers on every response, and no 503?

brief.where: POST /orders returns 201 with the order, or 401 for a missing header. The 20 enterprise integrations are automated and will see whatever surface you choose; nothing documents error shapes today.
brief.what: The exact rejection contract: status code, Retry-After, body shape, and whether allowed responses carry remaining-quota headers so integrations can self-pace.
brief.how: 429 with Retry-After is retriable by most clients and keeps 5xx meaning 'our fault'. 503 would be retried by generic backoff but pollutes error dashboards and contradicts a fail-open stance.

evidence.note: the only status codes in use today

risks: Integrations that retry immediately on 429 turn a throttle into a traffic amplifier.
Header-only signalling leaves integrations that ignore headers with no backoff signal.

options.label: 429 + Retry-After + JSON body + X-RateLimit-* always
options.description: Full contract, documented and emitted on success too
options.tradeoff: Gives automated clients everything needed to back off and self-pace; requires agreeing header names and a body shape you will support forever.
options.holds_when: You can publish the contract to the 20 integrations before enforcement.
options.cost: Docs page, one shared error helper, integration notices.

options.label: 429 with JSON body only
options.description: Status and message, no timing hints
options.tradeoff: Minimal surface to support; clients without Retry-After tend to retry immediately and amplify the load.
options.holds_when: Clients already implement exponential backoff on 4xx.

options.label: Accept and queue, return 202
options.description: Buffer writes instead of rejecting
options.tradeoff: Nothing to explain to customers; hides latency as client timeouts, needs a durable queue, and defeats the purpose if the queue drains into the same Postgres.
options.holds_when: Accepted writes can be persisted out of band, which this repo cannot do today.

questions.question: Should per-customer limits live in a Postgres table read with a 60s cache, owned by CS with audited on-call temporary overrides?

brief.where: PLAN.md leaves both the numbers and their owner undecided. There is no config file, admin surface, or customer metadata table in the repo, and no way to change a limit without a deploy today.
brief.what: Where per-customer limits live and who may change them, including at 3am during an incident. This also decides whether a bursty enterprise can be unblocked without a release.
brief.how: A Postgres table is auditable, reuses an existing dependency, and costs one cached read per minute. A static file is reviewable but needs a deploy. A Redis hash is instant but unaudited and creates a second source of truth next to the counters.

evidence.note: legitimate bursters and undecided ownership

risks: Unaudited runtime edits make 'why did this customer get 10x' unanswerable in a postmortem.
Deploy-gated limits mean an incident fix is blocked on a release train.

options.label: Postgres table, cached, CS-owned with override audit
options.description: customer_rate_limits(customer_id, rps, burst, updated_by, note)
options.tradeoff: Auditable, survives restarts, reuses the existing DB, and lets on-call raise a limit in seconds; costs a migration, a cache with a staleness window, and a named owner for the numbers.
options.holds_when: The enterprise list is small and changes are rare but urgent.
options.cost: One migration, one cache, one support runbook.

options.label: Static config per deploy
options.description: Limits in env or a committed file
options.tradeoff: Simplest to review and impossible to fat-finger at runtime; every limit change waits for a deploy, including during an incident.
options.holds_when: You can deploy on demand and the 20 numbers are stable for months.

options.label: Redis hash edited by on-call
options.description: Limits stored beside the counters
options.tradeoff: Instant changes and no migration; unaudited, easy to mistype, and lost if the keyspace is flushed by its real owner.
options.holds_when: Speed matters more than auditability for a week-long experiment.

brief.where: Response contract, override table, and store are settled, so enforcement and logging can be separated. Nothing exists today that would log a would-be rejection.

options.cost: One config flag, one log line, a few days of elapsed time.
options.description: Log would-be rejections; enforce cluster-wide after the numbers are validated
options.holds_when: You can tolerate a few extra days before the incident is structurally prevented.
options.label: Shadow for 3-5 days, then enforce everywhere
options.tradeoff: You learn the real per-customer distribution, including the 20 bursters, before any customer sees a 429; costs several days of exposure to a repeat incident and a second deploy.

options.description: Enable at a deliberately generous level, tighten weekly
options.holds_when: Only egregious traffic must stop immediately.
options.label: Enforce immediately at loose limits
options.tradeoff: Protection starts now and tuning is data-driven; the first numbers are a guess and a burster can still be caught by a bad one.

options.description: Enable per customer as each one confirms
options.holds_when: You can reach all 20 owners quickly.
options.label: Staged enablement per customer
options.tradeoff: Zero surprise for the integrations you talk to; requires tracking state per customer and a long tail of unconfirmed customers staying unprotected.

brief.what: What the limiter emits — per-customer decision counters, the degraded-mode gauge, Redis error rate — and which of those pages a human.
brief.where: There is no metrics or logging layer in the repo at all; the limiter's only current output would be a 429 body. Degraded mode was chosen deliberately, so it needs a signal.

options.cost: A metrics emitter, a dashboard, two alerts.
options.description: Counter per (customer, route, decision), gauge for degraded mode, alert on degraded > 1 min and on top-10 429 spikes
options.holds_when: You want the shadow period to actually produce numbers.
options.label: Per-customer decision counters + degraded gauge + two alerts
options.tradeoff: Makes both the tuning round and the incident review answerable; costs a metrics dependency the repo does not have and a card that needs a sample size decision.

options.description: One log line per rejection
options.holds_when: You will read logs manually during the shadow period.
options.label: Log lines only
options.tradeoff: No new dependency and enough to debug; nothing pages anyone and the degraded path is invisible unless someone greps.

options.description: 429 count and Redis errors, no per-customer dimension
options.holds_when: You only need to know that something is being throttled.
options.label: Aggregate counters only
options.tradeoff: Cheapest to add; cannot tell which customer is being limited, which is the one question both tuning and support will ask.
